title: Paper from Samarkand
hook: papermaking spreads west, and books become cheaper

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bayt al-Hikmah, the House of Wisdom, and Hunayn comparing his copies of Galen. Your line was: wisdom from everywhere. Who did you learn something from? Day nine hundred sixteen.

A receipt. A sticky note. The back of an envelope with a shopping list on it. Paper is so ordinary now that it gets thrown away by the handful. Yet for a long time, writing something down meant writing on something costly: the scraped and dried skin of an animal, or papyrus reeds that grew along the Nile. Every page had a price. Yesterday we watched Baghdad gather the world's books. All those translations, all those copies, needed something to be written on. The answer came from the east, by way of a city on the Silk Road called Samarkand. Today: warraqun, the paper people.
screen: `A RECEIPT, A STICKY NOTE.` → `ONCE, EVERY PAGE HAD A PRICE.` → `SOMETHING CAME FROM THE EAST.`

segments.voice: Paper came from China, made from plant fibers and rags beaten into pulp, spread thin on a screen, and dried. There's a story told by later writers about how it reached the Muslim world: that after a battle in Central Asia, Chinese prisoners were brought to Samarkand, and some of them knew how to make paper and taught the craft there. It's a good story. Historians question it, and some think the knowledge traveled more slowly, along trade routes. Either way, Samarkand paper became known, and before long paper was being made in Baghdad too. The historian Ibn Khaldun says that the Barmakid minister al-Fadl ibn Yahya, from the family we met with Harun, had government records written on paper. Now see what that did. Paper was cheaper than skin and easier to come by than papyrus. Cheaper paper meant cheaper books. Baghdad grew a market of booksellers and copyists, called warraqun, the paper people. The bookseller Ibn al-Nadim, whose catalog told us about al-Ma'mun's dream, was one of them. Scholars could own more books, students could copy their teachers' lectures, and the translations of the House of Wisdom could travel. The Qur'an speaks of God, in Pickthall's words, "Who teacheth by the pen." A pen needs a page. In this story, the page got cheap, and learning spread. Paper changed everything.
screen: `A CHINESE INVENTION.` · `THE STORY OF THE PRISONERS.` · `THE PAPER PEOPLE OF BAGHDAD.` · then, large: `WHO TEACHETH BY THE PEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: write on paper, thankfully. Find a sheet of paper and a pen, any kind. Hold the paper for a moment before you write. Feel how thin and light it is. Breathe in. Bring to mind the long chain behind it: the craft carried from China, the mills of Samarkand and Baghdad, the copyists in their market. Breathe out. Now write one line by hand, slowly. Something you're grateful for, or something you've learned this week. If you pray, you can begin with bismillah, as some Muslims do before writing. If you don't, just write with care. The bell holds the time.
Warraqun, the paper people: the booksellers and copyists who multiplied once paper reached Baghdad by way of Samarkand, making books cheaper and learning easier to share. Today's word.
Your line: paper changed everything. Today, before you throw a piece of paper away, pause and use the blank side for one more line. Day nine hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Historians of the book study surviving paper manuscripts from the Muslim world, and calligraphers today still prepare paper by hand for copying the Qur'an and other texts.
